title: Anselm's argument
hookLine: God is that than which nothing greater can be thought

cards: A monk is stuck. By his own account, he's been hunting for one single argument, short and complete, that would show God exists. It keeps slipping away.
He tries to give up on it, and it won't leave him alone. Then one day it arrives, and he writes it down. His name is Anselm, and the surprise is where he puts the argument.
Not in a lecture. In a prayer. The little book opens with Anselm talking to God, asking to see God's face.
Only then, mid-prayer, does he make his move.

teach.b: First, his reason for arguing at all. In words close to his: I don't seek to understand so that I can believe. I believe so that I can understand.
Faith, looking for understanding. Then he turns to a psalm: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God." He starts with a definition.
God is something than which nothing greater can be thought. Even the fool understands those words, so the idea is at least in his mind. Now a painter.
Before painting, the picture is in the painter's mind. After, it's in the mind and on the wall. Which is greater?

So if that-than-which-nothing-greater-can-be-thought existed only in the mind, you could think of something greater: the same thing, but real. And that can't be. So, Anselm concludes, it must exist in reality.

teach.h: THE PAINTER AND THE PERFECT ISLAND.
teach.b: A monk named Gaunilo wrote a reply on behalf of the fool: picture an island more perfect than any other; does that make it real? Anselm answered him, and the debate is still going among philosophers.
But a few chapters later comes one more turn, the source of today's line.
God, Anselm says, is not only that than which nothing greater can be thought. God is greater than can be thought. For Anselm, the argument isn't a fence around God.
It ends at an edge, with more past it than the mind can hold.

how: Christians meet Anselm's argument in philosophy and theology classes, where it is still argued for and against; some also read his Proslogion as a book of prayer.

o: a case that faith needs no reasons at all
a proof of God from the idea of the greatest
a proof of God from the order seen in nature

p: the fool says there is no God
picture in mind, then on the wall

s: Anselm wrote his argument as a dry lecture
he set it inside a prayer, talking to God before he makes his move.
Anselm says God is greater than can be thought
a few chapters after the argument, he says God is not only the greatest thinkable, but greater than can be thought.
everyone in Anselm's day accepted the argument
a monk named Gaunilo answered on behalf of the fool with a perfect island.

games.q: you're Anselm. Gaunilo says: by your logic, a perfect island would have to exist. what do you do?
o: write an answer and keep the argument.
games.why: Anselm wrote a reply to Gaunilo and kept his argument. the debate is still going among philosophers.

practice: Let your mind reach for the biggest, best thing it can hold: mountains, oceans, a love that never fails, the whole night sky.
Notice that whatever you've got, you can still think of something greater, and rest there, at the edge of your thinking. If you pray, you can turn toward God the way Anselm did, talking first.

wordCard.voice: Anselm's argument. God is that than which nothing greater can be thought, and, Anselm adds, greater than can be thought at all, an argument made inside a prayer.

orig.s: aliquid quo nihil maius cogitari possit
orig.say: AH-lee-kwid kwoh NEE-hil MY-yoos koh-gee-TAH-ree POS-sit
orig.note: Latin: something than which nothing greater can be thought, Anselm's definition of God in the Proslogion.

carryVoice: Your line: greater than can be thought. For Anselm, the edge of thinking was a place to pray. That's today, done.
